analysis.one_liner: Extends federal anti-discrimination protection to private contracts and to discriminatory seniority systems at work.
analysis.headline: The bill expanded workplace discrimination protections but never got a committee hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court narrowed federal job-discrimination law in cases like Patterson and Wards Cove, Senator Orrin Hatch introduced a bill to restore some of that protection. It would have made clear that workers can sue over discrimination by private parties in carrying out or ending a contract, and that a worker can challenge a workplace seniority system adopted for discriminatory reasons — even if the bias is not written into the rules — whenever that system injures them. The bill went to the Senate Labor Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and businesses subject to discrimination by private parties. The bill would have made clear that federal civil rights protections apply to private discrimination in the making, performance, breach, or termination of contracts — after the Supreme Court's Patterson decision had limited section 1981 to contract formation. It also would have let employees injured by a seniority system that was adopted for intentionally discriminatory reasons sue, even years after the system was adopted, addressing the limits the Court placed on such challenges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing discrimination in contracts and seniority

how_it_helps.text: It declared that federal contract rights protect against discrimination by private parties, not just by government actors, and that the protection covers discrimination in carrying out or ending a contract — not just in making one.

It let workers challenge a seniority system adopted for a discriminatory purpose — even when that purpose was not written into the rules — whenever they were injured by it, removing a time limit that had made such challenges difficult.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would have faced additional lawsuits over discriminatory contract practices and biased seniority systems, including systems adopted long ago.

drawbacks.text: It was narrower than the competing Civil Rights Act of 1990, which would have overturned more of the Wards Cove decision and made it easier to challenge any practice with a discriminatory effect; this bill limited relief to contracts and intentionally discriminatory seniority systems.

Allowing workers to challenge discriminatory seniority systems long after their adoption would have exposed employers to liability for longstanding pay and promotion structures, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed real legal gaps left by recent Supreme Court rulings, and its narrowness made it hard to attack as opening the door to quotas. But it was also far weaker than the competing civil rights bill of the same year, which would have restored broader standards for challenging employment practices. Its main drawback was that it left most workers to rely on the more restrictive post-Wards Cove legal framework, and its main cost was modest additional litigation for employers. As drafted, it offered genuine but limited protection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote before the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 22, 1990 by Senator Hatch with three Republican cosponsors, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
No further action was taken: it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and died in committee when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

It was introduced in the same Congress as the broader Civil Rights Act of 1990, the effort to overturn Supreme Court decisions including Wards Cove and Patterson; this bill was the Republican alternative focused on contracts and seniority systems.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers were better off: no one ever had to vote on it, and the harder-to-satisfy legal standards from the Supreme Court's recent decisions remained in place.

for.name: Sen. Orrin G. Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee.

for.name: 4 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Dole, Thurmond, Coats, and Hatch)

against.name: Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred: no hearing, no markup, and no vote before Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; the broader civil rights bill of 1990 was the Democratic-led alternative, and this narrower version drew no Democratic cosponsors in the record.

industries.industry: Employers and businesses that use seniority systems
industries.note: The bill would have let workers sue over seniority systems adopted for discriminatory reasons, even long after adoption, exposing employers to back-pay and promotion claims. Costs would fall mainly on large employers with entrenched promotion ladders.
The bill would have applied federal anti-discrimination guarantees to discrimination by private actors in carrying out or terminating contracts, expanding liability beyond government actors.
